newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian shares fall back after ringgit fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian shares fall back after ringgit fall.

text.p: Two days after achieving a shaky technical rebound, Malaysian share prices weakened on Friday afternoon as the ringgit slumped to its weakest post-flotation level, analysts and dealers said.
The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed 8.36 points, or 0.91 percent, lower at 910.18. It had peaked at 929.50 before the lunch break.
"It seems to be reacting to the ringgit's fall. There is a lot of negative reaction from Singapore," said a vice president of share index futures trading at a local brokerage house.
On Friday, the ringgit dipped to 2.8250 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest level since the currency was first floated in 1973, before recovering to 2.7780 at 1000 GMT.
The fresh round of selling on the ringgit came mainly from foreign funds out of Singapore, said analysts.
"The market is very, very nervous at the moment," said Tony Shue, vice president of dealing at Jupiter Securities.
Malaysia's Consumer Price Index for July grew by 2.1 percent from the same month in 1996, the Statistics Department said earlier.
But analysts said the release of the figure did not influence share prices significantly as it was overshadowed by the ringgit's fall.
Share prices had staged a strong technical rebound since Wednesday after several days of selling by foreign funds.
A Reuters poll of 10 research houses on Thursday showed the next support level for the Composite Index at the 874 point level, and the next resistance at 968.
At the close on Friday, market volume stood at 285 million shares, valued at 1.60 billion ringgit. Losers swamped gainers 451 to 179.

Among the hardest hit stocks were key blue-chips such as power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd, telecommunications utility Telekom Malaysia Bhd and gaming company Magnum Corporation Bhd, losing 20 cents each.
Conglomerate Sime Darby Bhd closed up five cents at 7.90 ringgit, but had earlier peaked at 7.95 ringgit.
Bucking the trend in the afternoon session was UMW Holdings Bhd, which held on to a 25 cent gain at 8.05 ringgit, after having peaked at 8.20 ringgit.
Analysts said the stock was trading at an average price-to-earnings ratio of six-times 1998 earnings, and based on its recent half-year earnings, was cheap.
"People have just realised that it is incredibly cheap at six-times 1998 earnings," said Chehan Perera, auto analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in Kuala Lumpur.
The company recorded a 69 percent increase in net earnings for the six months to June 30, 1997 compared to the same period in 1996.
Analysts said the outlook for stocks next week remained shaky with the focus likely to remain on the currency markets.
"Next week will still depend on the ringgit. If it slides down even further, we could see the index going to 885 or even 850," said the index futures vice president.
